title: The four immeasurables, now
tomorrow: can you give away the good you've done?

cards: Some group chats run on one question: whose version is right? Two young brahmins in the suttas, Vasettha and Bharadvaja, had that argument.
Each said his own teacher knew the straight road to union with Brahma, the god their tradition honored. They couldn't settle it, so they took it to the Buddha. Here's the strange part.
Union with Brahma was not the goal the Buddha taught. He could have waved the question away. Instead he gave them a road to Brahma.

teach.b: First, in the Tevijja Sutta, he asks them a question back: has any teacher of yours seen Brahma face to face? No, they admit. Then it's like building a staircase to a mansion no one has seen.
So he starts with what their own tradition says Brahma is like: free of hatred, free of ill will, master of himself. And he describes a heart that matches.
It fills one direction with kindness, then the second, the third, the fourth, then above, below, everywhere, with no edge.

Then the same with compassion, then gladness for others' good, then equanimity, a steadiness that doesn't tip. He compares it to a strong conch blower, heard in every direction at once. That's the puzzle solved.
He met them in their own words and moved the road inside: a heart like Brahma's is the way to Brahma.
That's the sense of the name Buddhists still use for these four: the brahmaviharas, Brahma's dwelling places.
Their other name is the four immeasurables: metta, karuna, mudita, upekkha.

Immeasurable because the sutta leaves no one out of them. Some readers find the third the hardest. Kindness to someone hurting comes easier than gladness for someone winning, especially when they won the thing you wanted.

how: Buddhists practice the four immeasurables by sending kindness, compassion, gladness and equanimity outward, often direction by direction or person by person, in sitting practice and in daily life.

o: four realms beyond the stars where the gods live
four rules a monk can never break without leaving
kindness, compassion, gladness and steadiness without limit

games.q: four ways of the heart — tap the pairs.

s: the Buddha told the brahmins their question about Brahma was pointless
he answered it, in their own words: a heart like Brahma's is the way to Brahma.
equanimity means not caring what happens to people
it's the fourth immeasurable, steadiness, sent out alongside kindness, not instead of it.
the brahmaviharas are named after Brahma
Brahma's dwelling places: the Tevijja story shows why the name fits.

games.q: you send kindness easily to friends, but skip the neighbor whose dog barks all night. what does 'immeasurable' ask of you here?
o: let the kindness reach him too: the sutta leaves no direction out.
kindness is for people who've earned it; friends first, the neighbor never.
equanimity covers him: stop noticing him, and no kindness is needed.
games.why: the sutta fills every direction, above, below, everywhere, with no edge. immeasurable means no one is left out.

practice: Find a photo with people in it and rest your eyes on one face. Give that face the four in turn: may you be well; may your pain ease; I'm glad for your good things; and whatever comes, may you stay steady.
Then move to the next face, and the next, the way the sutta moves from one direction to the next.

wordCard.voice: The four immeasurables: kindness, compassion, gladness and equanimity, a heart sent in every direction. Also called the brahmaviharas.

orig.note: Pali: appamanna, the immeasurables, without measure or limit.

carryVoice: Your line: immeasurable. Kindness with the edges taken off, gladness included, no one left out. Day ten of the summit.
